reading.body:
James Green's 31 AI lobbying filings are concentrated in telecommunications carriers, not in AI developers or data center operators.

The client list is CTIA, Lumen, Verizon, AT&T, IAC, and Match Group. Four of the six are telecom carriers or their trade association. That is the pattern the filings disclose: AI lobbying here runs through the companies that own the wires, the same companies whose networks and rights of way the buildout depends on. The bills named, S 2455, S 4407, S 2714, S 2750, HR 8516, S 2296, S 3062, S 1396, S 1269, S 3813, S 3495, HR 7757, and HR 7294, are not described in this data, so what each one would do to AI or to network infrastructure is not established here.

The filings are all dated 2025 or later, which makes this a current record rather than a historical one. Thirty-one filings across six clients means the activity is sustained, not a single registration. The firm channel matters too: 31 filings routed through one lobbying firm, uid fbd27b14, so the disclosure reflects an institutional practice rather than scattered individual registrations.

What this does not show is money, outcome, or position. LDA filings record that contact occurred and which bills were named, not what was said, what was spent, or whether anything changed. It also does not connect these clients to any specific AI data center, power purchase, or interconnection queue. The link between telecom lobbying and the grid constraint on AI is plausible from the client list alone, and this data does not prove it.
